submission.summary: This man has achalasia diagnosed in 2021 after six months of progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, mid-chest food sticking, and occasional regurgitation of undigested food without reported weight loss or vomiting. Upper endoscopy showed a dilated esophagus with retained food but no mass or stricture, and manometry demonstrated aperistalsis with incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation; achalasia remains on subsequent problem lists, with no treatment or symptom resolution documented. He also has alcohol use disorder with reported intake of approximately 6–8 beers daily for years, including daily beer use in 2024. In 2021, his liver was palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, AST was mildly elevated at 45 U/L, ALT was 52 U/L, and bilirubin was 1.2 mg/dL, without documented jaundice, ascites, or other signs of decompensation. In 2022, he had folate-deficiency macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, MCV 115 fL, folate 2 ng/mL) with glossitis, in the setting of heavy alcohol use and a poor diet; vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid were normal. Relevant comorbidities include obesity (BMI approximately 30–32 kg/m²), type 2 diabetes (historical HbA1c 7.8%), dyslipidemia, hypertension, gout, and nephrolithiasis. Most recently listed medications are metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily; no GI-directed therapy or folate replacement is documented, and he has no known drug allergies.

This 32-year-old man has had recurrent emergency visits for traumatic and occupational injuries, most recently after a motorcycle crash in July 2021 with right arm and leg weakness and sensory loss. Examination showed 3/5 right-sided strength, reduced right proprioception, vibration and light touch below approximately T10, and reduced left pain and temperature below T12; spinal MRI showed a right hemicord lesion at T10, consistent with traumatic Brown-Séquard syndrome. Reflexes were normal, and he reported no bowel or bladder incontinence; CBC and electrolytes were normal and toxicology was negative. In January 2020, another motorcycle crash caused left lower-leg arterial occlusion treated with embolectomy, followed by severe pain with passive movement, swelling, pallor, weak distal pulses, sensory loss and inability to move the toes, concerning for acute compartment syndrome or persistent limb ischemia. At that time CK was 2,500 U/L, myoglobin 150 ng/mL, potassium 5.2 mEq/L and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, raising concern for muscle injury and hyperkalemia. In July 2020, a high-pressure paint-gun puncture to the left palm caused marked pain, swelling and pain on passive finger extension despite a small entry wound; hand radiographs showed no bony injury, WBC was 12,000/µL and creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL. His surgical history also records right-hand fasciotomy for crush-related compartment syndrome, although the documented acute hand injection injury was left-sided. He takes no documented medications, has no known drug allergies, is a former smoker, drinks alcohol socially and works as an automotive spray painter.

This man has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), diagnosed in 2020 after bilateral flank masses and an abdominal ultrasound showing multiple bilateral renal cysts; his father reportedly had ADPKD with end-stage kidney disease. At diagnosis, creatinine was 1.2 mg/dL, with no later kidney-function results, urine studies, or documented renal replacement therapy available. Blood pressure was 155/95 mmHg on two measurements in 2020, with a mildly elevated aldosterone level and a left upper-quadrant bruit, although it was 124/78 mmHg in 2022 and no antihypertensive is listed. Nephrology-relevant comorbidities include ongoing tobacco use and Buerger disease with progressive digital ischemia and ulcers. He also has alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with basilar-predominant emphysema, for which he uses as-needed albuterol. He has used ibuprofen 400–600 mg as needed, reported as occasional use in 2024, when he presented with a guaiac-positive gastric ulcer and dark stools; NSAID exposure is pertinent to both kidney and gastrointestinal risk. No disease-specific ADPKD therapy is documented, and the most recent encounter describes normal vital signs but provides no updated renal labs.

This male patient has bipolar I disorder with recurrent manic episodes and psychotic features, as well as schizotypal personality disorder. In January 2025, he presented after 10 days of sleeping only 1–2 hours nightly, pressured and tangential speech, irritability, impulsive spending, grandiose claims about a satellite-communication device, and paranoid beliefs that government agents were tracking him; a similar episode with reduced sleep, spending, and persecutory beliefs occurred in 2022, with an earlier hospitalization also reported. Following a week-long psychiatric admission for acute mania with psychosis, he returned to the ED approximately five hours after his first dose of a newly prescribed, unnamed high-potency antipsychotic with jaw spasm, painful cervical muscle contraction, and upward eye deviation, strongly suggestive of an acute dystonic reaction with oculogyric crisis. His longstanding schizotypal features include social detachment, eccentric dress and speech, magical beliefs, and unusual perceptual experiences, without sustained psychosis documented at his baseline assessment. Recorded home mood stabilizers are lithium carbonate 300 mg orally twice daily and lamotrigine 100 mg orally daily; no lithium level, renal function, or current thyroid monitoring results are available. Urine toxicology was negative during both manic presentations; earlier CBC and thyroid studies were normal, while laboratory testing at the dystonia visit was pending. He reports no illicit substance use, never smoking, and infrequent social alcohol use, with no other established medical comorbidity or known drug allergies documented. Family psychiatric history includes bipolar I disorder in his father, depression in his mother, and psychotic-spectrum or schizotypal illness in an uncle.

This 4-year-old girl has oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, diagnosed in January 2020 after two months of right-knee swelling, intermittent fever, morning limping, and pain with walking. At rheumatology evaluation, the knee was warm, swollen, and limited in range of motion; other joints were unremarkable, with no rash, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly. ESR was 40 mm/hr and CRP 2.5 mg/dL; ANA was positive and rheumatoid factor negative. She is treated with naproxen suspension 125 mg orally twice daily with food, with no other rheumatologic medications documented. Her July 2020 pediatric examination was unremarkable, although joint-specific disease activity was not documented. No other medical comorbidities are recorded; immunizations are up to date and she has no known drug allergies. Family history includes maternal autoimmune hypothyroidism and rheumatoid arthritis in a maternal aunt. Given ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA, ophthalmologic screening for asymptomatic uveitis is relevant, but no screening results are documented.

This 26-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of acute urticaria, first evaluated by Dermatology in January 2020 and recurring in September 2020. She develops pruritic, raised erythematous wheals on the trunk and arms; individual lesions resolve within a day while new ones appear. Examination documented well-demarcated, variably sized plaques, some with a pale halo, that blanch with pressure, without other skin changes. No preceding infection, new medication, or dietary trigger was identified, and she denied angioedema, breathing difficulty, abdominal pain, fever, and arthralgia. Her past medical history is otherwise unremarkable, although her mother has seasonal allergic rhinitis and her father has asthma. January 2020 CBC, metabolic panel, and TSH were normal, and serum tryptase was not elevated. She reports taking no medications and has no known drug allergies; she has never smoked and drinks alcohol socially.

This man has biopsy-confirmed non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) diagnosed in 2022 after presenting with persistent cough and a 15-pound unintentional weight loss. Chest CT at diagnosis showed a 4-cm right upper lobe mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy; a separate 6-mm noncalcified right lower lobe nodule had been identified on screening CT in 2020. In January 2024, he presented with further weight loss (approximately 7 kg over two months), persistent cough with blood-streaked sputum, poor appetite, lethargy, and confusion; chest imaging again showed a lung mass, described as central. The available record does not document cancer staging, molecular testing, metastatic evaluation, or receipt of surgery, radiation, or systemic anticancer therapy. Relevant comorbidities include COPD and ongoing tobacco use with a 30-pack-year history; he had a hypoxemic, hypercapnic COPD exacerbation in July 2023. At the 2022 cancer evaluation, hemoglobin was 14 g/dL, WBC 7,000/µL, platelets 250,000/µL, sodium 140 mEq/L, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL; no laboratory evaluation of the 2024 confusion is available. His documented medications are tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled daily and albuterol inhaled as needed, and he has no known allergies.

This woman has two major orthopedic issues: left knee osteoarthritis status post total knee arthroplasty and painful osseous metastases from progressive invasive ductal breast cancer. At orthopedic follow-up in 2020, mobility was improving with physical therapy and she walked with a cane; no implant complication was documented, and she was concerned about whether an alternative prosthetic material would improve outcomes. In 2021, persistent atraumatic right arm pain and focal humeral tenderness corresponded to a midshaft lytic lesion on radiographs, creating concern for a pathologic fracture; associated findings included normocytic anemia and elevated calcium. Her metastatic disease subsequently progressed despite multiple systemic treatments, with limited walking tolerance and recurrent malignancy-associated hypercalcemia (calcium 13.4 mg/dL with suppressed PTH in July 2022), treated with IV fluids and pamidronate; she also has a history of bisphosphonate infusions for skeletal disease. Advanced chronic kidney disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism further complicate bone health: January 2022 labs showed creatinine 9.1 mg/dL, BUN 75 mg/dL, phosphorus 6.8 mg/dL, PTH 600 pg/mL, and calcium 9.2 mg/dL, with painful necrotic calf lesions concerning for calciphylaxis. Type 2 diabetes with polyneuropathy, nephropathy, and previously elevated A1c (8.1%) adds fall, wound-healing, and perioperative risk; vitamin B12 deficiency and hyperlipidemia are additional comorbidities. Orthopedically relevant recorded therapies include anastrozole, sevelamer, calcitriol, insulin glargine/lispro, metformin, pioglitazone, and as-needed acetaminophen; she has no known drug allergies.

This man has active severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), confirmed by polysomnography in 2021 with an apnea–hypopnea index of 35/hour. Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, fragmented sleep, daytime sleepiness, fatigue, morning headaches, and impaired concentration have persisted across several visits; no CPAP use or other OSA treatment is documented. His low mood, irritability, and cognitive slowing were reassessed in 2022, when PHQ-9 was 10 and the neurologic examination was normal; the chart subsequently lists depressive disorder due to hypercalcemia. Obesity (BMI 32–35), a thick neck, crowded oropharynx, and retrognathia increase his sleep-apnea risk. Relevant comorbidities include primary hyperparathyroidism with recurrent calcium-oxalate stones, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and a 2025 inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction, alongside ongoing cigarette smoking. In 2021, hemoglobin was 18.5 g/dL, hematocrit 54.5%, and erythropoietin elevated, raising concern for secondary erythrocytosis in the setting of OSA; TSH was normal in 2020 and 2022. Most recent HbA1c was 7.8%, total cholesterol 220 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.2 mg/dL in 2025; calcium was 10.2 mg/dL and PTH 65 pg/mL in 2023. Documented home medications are metformin, lisinopril, amlodipine, chlorthalidone, atorvastatin, omeprazole, and as-needed calcium carbonate; no neurologic or psychiatric medication is recorded, and he has no known drug allergies.

This 3-year-old boy has recurrent acute otitis media, including a documented right-sided episode on January 15, 2020, followed by worsening right otalgia and fever at an ED visit on February 15. At the January visit, the right tympanic membrane was bulging, erythematous, and poorly mobile, with a normal left ear and no otorrhea. At the ED visit, he had three days of worsening pain, irritability, reduced appetite, and fever to 38.9°C; the right tympanic membrane remained bulging and erythematous. New right mastoid erythema and tenderness with anterior displacement of the auricle raise strong concern for acute mastoiditis complicating right acute otitis media. His WBC was 15,000/mm³ and CRP 40 mg/L; no imaging or microbiology results are documented. His history notes multiple prior antibiotic courses for recurrent otitis media, although the January note reported none in the preceding three months; no current antibiotic regimen is recorded. He takes acetaminophen suspension 160 mg/5 mL, 5 mL orally every 4–6 hours as needed for pain or fever, and has no known drug allergies or prior surgery. His father had recurrent otitis media requiring childhood tympanostomy tubes, his paternal uncle has chronic eustachian tube dysfunction, and there is no reported secondhand smoke exposure or other documented comorbidity relevant to ENT care.

This 35-year-old man has a critical-care presentation in January 2022 with fever, headache, confusion, and tingling at a bat-scratch site two months after exposure without medical evaluation, concerning for symptomatic rabies encephalitis. He was febrile to 38.9°C, tachycardic to 110 bpm, agitated and encephalopathic, with hypersalivation, difficulty swallowing water, and hyperreflexia; CSF showed lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and protein, but no confirmatory rabies test or treatment is documented. His WBC was 11,000/µL, while hemoglobin, platelets, electrolytes, glucose, BUN, and creatinine were essentially normal. In March 2021 he presented to the ED with acute dyspnea and left chest pain, tachycardia, and room-air SpO₂ 92%; chest radiography showed bowel loops in the left thorax and rightward mediastinal shift, consistent with a traumatic left diaphragmatic hernia, with no repair documented. In April 2020 he had positional right-sided clear rhinorrhea after a motor vehicle collision; positive nasal-fluid beta-2 transferrin supported a traumatic CSF leak, with no documented resolution. Other trauma history includes healed rib fractures, resolved pulmonary contusion, and mild traumatic brain injury. He has documented susceptibility to hepatitis A after no recorded vaccination, despite normal liver tests; hepatitis B vaccination is reported. He takes only a daily multivitamin, has no known drug allergies or prior surgery documented, has never smoked, and drinks approximately 2–3 alcoholic beverages per week.

This 66-year-old man has chronic kidney disease with a reported baseline creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL, as well as hypertension complicated by a January 2024 hypertensive emergency. During that admission, creatinine was 2.8 mg/dL and BUN 55 mg/dL, compared with a creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL documented during a January 2023 hematuria evaluation; CKD etiology, stage, and proteinuria are not documented. After 48 hours of intravenous sodium nitroprusside, he developed agitation, confusion, headache, flushing, and increased respiratory effort, with lactate 5 mmol/L and a pending cyanide level, raising concern for nitroprusside toxicity in the setting of renal impairment. At that time BP was 145/90 mmHg, sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, and arterial pH 7.35. He previously had gross initial-stream hematuria with urinary red cells but no casts, normal coagulation studies, and no flank tenderness, in the setting of BPH and a history of urethral stricture treated by cystoscopy and dilation. His home medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, and as-needed acetaminophen; no NSAID use is documented. Other relevant comorbidities include primary myelofibrosis with historical anemia/pancytopenia, Paget disease of bone, chronic bronchitis, and mild cognitive impairment; calcium, phosphorus, PTH, and vitamin D were normal in 2020 despite elevated alkaline phosphatase.

This 72-year-old man has recurrent, painless gastrointestinal bleeding attributed to cecal angiodysplasia, with intermittent bright red blood per rectum and, more recently, maroon stools. A tagged red blood cell scan localized bleeding to the cecum in 2022, and colonoscopy during active bleeding showed small, flat ectatic vascular lesions there; colonoscopies between episodes have not identified an active source. In January 2023, recurrent hematochezia was accompanied by hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, while abdominal CT angiography and repeat colonoscopy were unrevealing. In July 2023, he presented with fatigue, dyspnea and maroon stool on rectal examination; hemoglobin was 9.8 g/dL, and upper endoscopy and colonoscopy found no source. He has iron-deficiency anemia related to recurrent blood loss, with hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 15 ng/mL and serum iron 30 µg/dL in 2022. Severe aortic stenosis may contribute to recurrent angiodysplasia bleeding; his mechanical mitral valve requires warfarin (listed INR goal 2.5–3.5), and he also takes aspirin 81 mg, both important to bleeding and procedural management, although the July 2023 INR was 1.0. Other GI-relevant history includes chronic constipation treated intermittently with over-the-counter stool softeners and prior colonic polyps/polypectomy; there is no reported family history of colorectal cancer. Comorbid stage 3 chronic kidney disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia are relevant to GI care; July 2023 BUN was 28 mg/dL and creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, and other home medications include metformin, lisinopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin.

A 22-year-old man has recurrent major trauma, most recently a May 2021 head-on collision with hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, and concern for hemorrhagic shock. He had left upper quadrant tenderness with guarding and a positive FAST examination for intraperitoneal free fluid, concerning for intra-abdominal hemorrhage; blood pressure fell from 90/60 to 85/55 mmHg despite initial fluids. Hemoglobin was 9 g/dL versus a reported baseline of 14 g/dL, and oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. In September 2020, a high-speed collision caused an unstable pelvic fracture with lower abdominal and perineal ecchymosis, hypotension, tachycardia, hemoglobin 9 g/dL, and a negative FAST examination. In January 2020, a left chest stab wound caused a large traumatic left hemothorax with hypovolemic shock, absent left breath sounds, mediastinal shift, blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, and hemoglobin 8 g/dL. Platelets were 250,000/mm³ and coagulation studies normal at the 2020 pelvic-trauma encounter. He reports no medications and has no known drug allergies; he smokes one pack daily and reports heavy episodic drinking three to four times weekly.

This 70-year-old man has hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a documented type A aortic dissection in January 2024, with emergency repair listed in his surgical history. At the dissection presentation, he had abrupt tearing chest pain radiating to the back with syncope, blood pressure 180/95 mmHg in the right arm versus 165/90 in the left, a diastolic murmur, diminished femoral pulse, and a widened mediastinum on chest radiograph; ECG showed no ischemia and troponin I was normal. His atrial fibrillation is treated with apixaban 5 mg twice daily, and aspirin 81 mg daily is also listed; no rate- or rhythm-control agent is documented. Antihypertensives listed are lisinopril 20 mg daily and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily. Parkinson disease with autonomic dysfunction complicates blood-pressure management: previously, seated BP fell from 145/85 to 120/70 mmHg on standing without a compensatory heart-rate increase. Long-standing poorly controlled type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, former smoking (20 pack-years), and a maternal history of abdominal aortic aneurysm add cardiovascular risk. Most recent available labs in January 2025 showed creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, and magnesium 1.6 mg/dL, with the low electrolytes relevant to arrhythmia risk and diuretic use. Other relevant comorbidities include neurogenic bladder and recurrent bowel dysmotility/volvulus; he also takes carbidopa/levodopa, pramipexole, selegiline, and oxybutynin.

A 67-year-old man with moderate-to-severe COPD and ongoing tobacco use (40 pack-years, currently ½ pack/day) presented to the ED in July 2020 with two days of worsening dyspnea and yellow sputum, consistent with a recurrent COPD exacerbation. He was tachypneic (RR 28) with accessory muscle use, diffuse wheezes and basilar crackles, and hypoxemic to 89% on room air. His room-air arterial blood gas showed pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 55 mmHg, PaO₂ 60 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 26 mEq/L, indicating acidemia with hypercapnia and hypoxemia; earlier blood gases documented chronic CO₂ retention (PaCO₂ 50–58 mmHg). He was also tachycardic to 130 with an irregularly irregular pulse; ECG showed at least four distinct P-wave morphologies, consistent with multifocal atrial tachycardia, without acute ischemic changes. He had a similar ED presentation in April 2020 with green sputum, low-grade fever and room-air saturation of 89%; chest radiography then showed hyperinflation without consolidation. Progressive exertional dyspnea had been noted at a January 2020 medicine visit, and his chart also lists prior hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis attributed to excess normal saline infusion; renal function was reportedly normal at that time. Home inhalers include tiotropium, fluticasone/salmeterol 250/50 mcg twice daily and albuterol as needed; he has no known drug allergies.

This woman has hidradenitis suppurativa, evaluated by Dermatology in 2020 for recurrent painful axillary and groin nodules and abscesses with sinus tracts; topical clindamycin 1% gel twice daily remains listed for HS and acne. She returned to Dermatology in 2021 for progressive crown hair thinning, with concurrent facial hirsutism and a history of acne. Polycystic ovary syndrome with irregular menses, prior infertility, and elevated total testosterone (82 ng/dL in 2020–2021) provides a relevant hyperandrogenic context for her hair and acne concerns. Acanthosis nigricans of the neck and obesity (recorded BMI 32–36 kg/m²) suggest insulin resistance; she takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, although fasting glucose was 96–98 mg/dL, lipids were normal, and TSH was normal. She was pregnant at the last documented encounter in October 2023, an important consideration in selecting dermatologic treatments. Other relevant history includes irritable bowel syndrome, recurrent UTIs treated with daily nitrofurantoin, prior cholecystectomy, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, and acute cholangitis; she is a former smoker and has no known drug allergies. Her October 2023 evaluation for fatigue, dark urine, and icterus showed marked liver injury (AST 850 U/L, ALT 920 U/L, bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL), which is important before considering systemic dermatologic therapy. Other listed medications are a prenatal vitamin and as-needed dicyclomine; no systemic HS or alopecia treatment is documented.

This 65-year-old man with GOLD IV COPD on continuous 2 L/min home oxygen and inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol, tiotropium, and as-needed albuterol has recurrent serious pulmonary infection. In January 2020 he presented with fever, purulent sputum, and dyspnea; chest radiography showed right lower-lobe consolidation and a small pleural effusion, and the chart subsequently described an opportunistic pulmonary infection requiring diagnostic sampling without identifying an organism. Thoracentesis yielded cloudy, exudative fluid (protein 4.0 g/dL versus serum 6.5, LDH 200 U/L versus serum 190) with pH 7.45, glucose 90 mg/dL, and 500 leukocytes/µL. In March he had increased green sputum and worsening respiratory status with somnolence, oxygen saturation 88% on 4 L/min, and severe hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.19, PCO₂ 76 mm Hg), raising concern for another infectious COPD exacerbation, although no pathogen was documented. His July 2020 ICU admission was for severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring mechanical ventilation, complicated by persistent hypotension and hypothermia; low T3, elevated reverse T3, slightly low TSH, and low-normal T4 were measured during critical illness. Pulmonary hypertension, type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, hypertension treated with lisinopril, GERD treated with omeprazole, and a 50-pack-year former smoking history are relevant comorbidities and exposures. Penicillin causes hives, which matters for antibiotic selection; iodinated contrast causes urticaria. No antimicrobial treatment, culture results, or identified causative organism are documented in the available record.

This 28-year-old man has an acute deformed femur after a severe July 2021 motor vehicle collision, concerning for a femoral fracture; the chart does not document dedicated femur imaging, fracture characterization, or orthopedic treatment. He was unconscious and in shock (BP 80/50 mmHg, pulse 130/min) with a distended abdomen, raising concern for major associated hemorrhage before orthopedic intervention. Hemoglobin was 6.0 g/dL and hematocrit 18%, with platelets 250,000/µL. He is a Jehovah’s Witness with a reported history of refusing transfusions, but has no documented advance directive and currently lacks decision-making capacity, making blood-management decisions especially important. Prior orthopedic trauma includes a radiographically confirmed right clavicle fracture after a January 2020 bicycle accident, associated with a small right pneumothorax and traumatic right subclavian vessel injury; healing status and treatment are not documented. He also sustained a left tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic instability in an October 2020 collision. No current or historical medications are listed, and he has no known drug allergies; he is a never-smoker with only occasional alcohol use.

This 25-year-old man has a documented oculogyric crisis after starting haloperidol in February 2020, with acute sustained upward eye deviation and neck stiffness consistent with medication-induced acute dystonia; haloperidol is listed as an adverse reaction. No recurrent eye deviation, visual symptoms, primary ocular disease, ophthalmic treatment, or eye examination findings are documented. His major comorbidity is treatment-resistant schizophrenia, with improvement in hallucinations and delusions on clozapine 300 mg daily at the July 2023 follow-up; docusate 100 mg daily is also listed. He has a history of agranulocytosis following trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment for a skin abscess, presenting with fever and oral ulcers in January 2023; that antibiotic is listed as an adverse reaction. July 2023 blood counts remained abnormal, with WBC 3,200/mm³ and ANC 800/mm³, while hemoglobin was 14 g/dL and platelets 250,000/mm³. The neutropenia and clozapine exposure are relevant to infection risk and coordination of care if ocular infection or an ophthalmic procedure arises. He reports no tobacco or alcohol use.

This 54-year-old woman has hypertension treated with lisinopril and recurrent left-leg deep vein thrombosis, with ultrasound-confirmed popliteal DVT in January 2020 after prolonged car travel and a subsequent documented iliofemoral DVT in July 2020 after a transatlantic flight. The July episode involved calf and thigh pain and swelling, with an elevated D-dimer; her father also had DVT. No anticoagulant is listed in the available medication records, so her current anticoagulation status needs clarification. Cardiovascular risk factors and relevant comorbidities include type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and rheumatoid arthritis treated with chronic prednisone 5 mg daily; she has never smoked and reports modest alcohol use. During a January 2021 ICU presentation for acute abdominal pain and vomiting after a fall, she remained hypotensive at 85/50 mmHg and tachycardic at 110 bpm despite initial saline resuscitation. At that presentation, sodium was 130 mEq/L, potassium 5.5 mEq/L, BUN 25 mg/dL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, and glucose 92 mg/dL, pertinent to hemodynamic and lisinopril management. Creatinine had been 1.0 mg/dL and the CBC normal during the July 2020 DVT admission. The available record documents no coronary disease, heart failure, arrhythmia, or cardiac testing; she has no known drug allergies.

This 30-year-old woman’s only documented active cardiovascular-related problem is gestational hypertension, described during pregnancy as mild, without proteinuria, and managed with dietary modification rather than medication. At her January 2022 ED evaluation for contractions, blood pressure was 138/88 mmHg and heart rate was 88 bpm; the chart does not document hypertensive emergency or cardiovascular symptoms. No chronic hypertension, structural heart disease, arrhythmia, coronary disease, or heart failure is documented. Her mother had preeclampsia, a relevant pregnancy-related risk factor. She has never smoked and reports no alcohol use. Her only recorded home medication is a daily prenatal vitamin; she has no documented antihypertensive therapy and has no known drug allergies. Other documented history includes carpal tunnel syndrome; no renal function, electrolytes, urine protein quantification, lipid panel, or other cardiometabolic laboratory results are available in the provided record. The available encounters are from 2020–2022, so current blood pressure and persistence or resolution of hypertension after pregnancy are unknown.

This 27-year-old woman has documented iron deficiency anemia, cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). In January 2020 she had symptomatic microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, MCV 72 fL) in the setting of heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and restrictive eating with frequent meal skipping; she takes a multivitamin with iron only sporadically. During a November 2021 admission following an upper respiratory illness, she presented with fatigue, orthostatic lightheadedness, exertional dyspnea, dark urine, scleral icterus, and mild splenomegaly. Her hemoglobin was 8.2 g/dL with MCV 90 fL, reticulocytes 8%, indirect hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL), elevated LDH, and undetectable haptoglobin, consistent with the charted hemolytic anemia; urinalysis showed no hematuria. Her AIP history includes abdominal cramps, distal sensory changes, dark urine, and mild hyponatremia in 2020; her maternal grandmother also had AIP, and restrictive eating and medication exposures are relevant to porphyria care. Other pertinent history includes recurrent upper respiratory infections, a maternal history of systemic lupus erythematosus, and a 2022 episode of right-sided Bell palsy following a cold. Her only documented home medications are the intermittently taken iron-containing multivitamin and ibuprofen 400 mg every six hours as needed for menstrual cramps; she has no known drug allergies and reports no tobacco or alcohol use. No malignancy, hematologic-directed therapy, or more recent blood counts are documented in the available record.

This 17-year-old female has type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin glargine 24 units subcutaneously nightly and insulin lispro dosed at 1 unit per 10 g carbohydrate with meals. She has had three documented episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis (January and April 2020 and January 2021), associated with intercurrent flu-like illness and difficulty taking insulin or missed doses during a busy school schedule. During the 2020 episodes, glucose was 550 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.1, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and urine ketones were positive; potassium was 5.2–5.5 mEq/L. In January 2021, glucose was 480 mg/dL, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, anion gap 25 mEq/L, elevated β-hydroxybutyrate, and 4+ urine ketones, again consistent with DKA. Her April 2020 DKA was accompanied by dehydration and BUN 30 mg/dL/creatinine 1.2 mg/dL; in January 2021, BUN was 18 mg/dL and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, with no urine protein reported. Her most recent documented encounter, in July 2022, was for severe bacterial meningitis with fever, hypotension, altered orientation, purpura, and CSF gram-negative diplococci, an acute illness relevant to glucose and insulin management; no concurrent serum glucose or metabolic panel is documented. Family history includes maternal autoimmune hypothyroidism and paternal type 2 diabetes, with no thyroid disorder documented in the patient. No HbA1c, outpatient glucose trends, or chronic microvascular diabetes complications are documented, and she has no known drug allergies.

This 27-year-old woman has an active lymphoma concerning for classical Hodgkin lymphoma: a February 2020 excisional supraclavicular lymph-node biopsy showed Reed–Sternberg cells, although no definitive subtype or stage is documented. Since late 2019 she has had progressive painless cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy with fevers, night sweats, and approximately 5 kg of unintentional weight loss. At her April 2020 ED visit, she additionally had palpable cervical and axillary nodes, worsening cough and positional dyspnea, chest discomfort and generalized pruritus after alcohol consumption, with decreased right upper-lung breath sounds. Chest radiographs showed mediastinal widening in January and a mediastinal mass in April, although the February radiograph was reported as unremarkable; no staging CT or PET is documented. Her February ESR was elevated at 50 mm/h, and April testing showed WBC 12,000/µL, eosinophils 10%, and LDH 350 U/L, with preserved hemoglobin (12.5 g/dL) and platelets (250,000/µL). She has no other documented medical comorbidities, takes no medications, has no known drug allergies, and has no documented lymphoma-directed therapy. Relevant family history includes a paternal cousin diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma at age 26 and a maternal aunt with breast cancer; she has never smoked and drinks 2–3 glasses of wine per week.

This 52-year-old woman has a charted history of left invasive ductal breast carcinoma, diagnosed by core biopsy in 2022 after a 2.1-cm spiculated mass was found; the tumor was ER-positive, PR-positive, and HER2-negative. Subsequent records document left modified radical mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy, but do not provide nodal pathology, stage, systemic treatment, or current surveillance status. She also has a history of pancreatic tumor resection and a 2024 problem-list entry for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor localization; weight loss, diarrhea, characteristic annular skin lesions, fasting glucose 180 mg/dL, and glucagon 600 pg/mL raise concern for an active glucagon-secreting tumor, although definitive localization and treatment are not documented.
